product: Ride matching & dispatch (driver location ingest + rider request matching)
summary: Driver apps stream their GPS position every few seconds into a geospatial index sharded by S2 cells, while rider requests flow through a demand service into DISCO, the dispatch optimizer. DISCO picks drivers by road-network ETA rather than straight-line distance, and once a trip is offered and accepted, a push platform keeps both parties' apps in sync.

scale.notes: The geospatial index was designed for about 1M location writes/sec, with reads at several times that (Uber's 2015 QCon talk, as summarised by HighScalability). Ride requests are a small fraction of this, estimated at a few thousand per second. The push layer handled over 250k messages/sec across more than 1.5M connections. All replica counts are estimates.

product: Video playback start via Open Connect CDN
summary: Everything before the play button runs on AWS. When a member presses play, the playback services check entitlement and licensing, choose stream assets, and ask a steering service which Open Connect Appliances should serve the session. The video bytes then come from OCAs, which are usually embedded inside the viewer's ISP and filled ahead of demand.

scale.notes: Estimate for play-start (control-plane) requests. In 2016 Netflix reported about 125M viewing hours a day and tens of Tbps at peak, all delivered by Open Connect. Chunk requests to OCAs are orders of magnitude higher than play-starts. Replica counts are estimates.

summary: Each phone keeps a persistent connection to an Erlang chat server, a heavily modified ejabberd fork on FreeBSD, where every connection is a lightweight process. The sending node looks up where the recipient is connected and forwards the message across the Erlang mesh. If the recipient is offline, the message is held until they reconnect and a push notification wakes them. Media goes separately to HTTP upload servers, and the chat message carries only a link and a thumbnail.

scale.notes: Estimate. In 2014 WhatsApp handled 50B messages/day, about 580k/s on average. Later public claims of 100B+/day give over 1.1M/s average, so the peak is estimated at about 2x that. One server held 2M+ connections (2012), and the fleet had 'hundreds of nodes' and over 8,000 cores in 2014. Replica counts are estimates.

product: Home feed load (feed API + photo fetch)
summary: Instagram's web tier is a large Django/Python fleet running under uWSGI. Feeds, stories and activity live in Cassandra; users, media and follow relationships live in PostgreSQL behind memcache. When someone posts, async Celery workers fed by RabbitMQ do the fan-out work. Images are fetched separately from a CDN.

scale.notes: Estimate: about 1B daily users times ~20 feed fetches a day gives ~230k/s average, so the peak is estimated at about 2x. The 2016 QCon deck reported 300M daily users, 95M uploads/day and memcache at 'millions of reads/writes per second'. Replica counts are estimates.

product: Video watch: metadata page + video bytes from edge cache
summary: A watch request has two halves. Front ends assemble the page and player config from cached objects, video metadata held in Vitess-sharded MySQL, and thumbnails in Bigtable. DNS then steers the player to a Google Global Cache node, often inside the viewer's ISP, which serves popular videos locally and fetches misses from Google's core.

scale.notes: Estimate for watch/playback-start requests. Early figures were 1B views/day (~11.6k/s). Today's volume is several times higher, so the estimate is ~5B views/day (~58k/s average) with about a 2x peak. Segment fetches to the CDN are far higher. Replica counts are estimates.

summary: Home timelines are precomputed when a tweet is written: a fan-out service pushes tweet IDs into each follower's timeline list in a replicated Redis cluster. A read then just fetches that list and hydrates the IDs through the tweet and user services, which sit behind memcache, so reads cost tens of milliseconds.

scale.notes: About 300K QPS of timeline reads (2013 figures, HighScalability). Writes ran ~5-7k tweets/s on average, with a 143,199 tweets/s one-second record in 2013 (InfoQ). Replica counts are estimates.

summary: A checkout page is assembled by a renderer that calls many backend services, each bound by a 99.9th-percentile latency SLA. The shopping cart sits on Dynamo, which is designed so 'add to cart' writes are never refused, with conflicting versions merged on read. Placing an order writes to the order store and hands fulfilment off asynchronously through queues.

scale.notes: Estimate. Prime Day 2023 saw 375M+ items bought on day one, about 4.3k items/s on average, and the estimate allows for peaks plus cart and checkout calls. Platform-wide context from AWS: DynamoDB peaked at 126M req/s, SQS at 86M msg/s and CloudFront at over 500M HTTP requests/min. The Dynamo paper reports 3M+ checkouts/day in 2007. Replica counts are estimates.

summary: A search goes to a root service that fans it out to sharded leaf services. Each leaf filters its slice of homes with an embedding-based retrieval step on a Lucene index, scores the survivors with a deep model, and checks live price and availability. The root merges the leaf results and runs a final setwise re-ranker. Listing embeddings are computed offline every day, so only the query embedding is calculated per request.

scale.notes: Estimate of a few thousand searches/s, based on traffic levels. The EBR paper says the system scores millions of homes per second, popular markets have about 100k eligible homes, and listings update at about 10k/s. Replica counts are estimates.

summary: When a user hits play, the client asks Spotify's backend, which runs largely as microservices on Google Cloud, for track metadata and a location for the encrypted audio file. A 2010 Spotify paper reported a median playback latency of about 265 ms; I didn't open it, so it isn't cited. Replica counts are estimates.

summary: A message is posted to the Python API monolith, which persists it through Rust data services into ScyllaDB and hands it to the guild's Elixir process. Each guild process knows every connected session in that server and publishes the event to all of them, using Manifold to batch sends per remote node. Session processes then push the event down each client's WebSocket.

scale.notes: Estimate for message sends/s. Sources: nearly 5M concurrent users and millions of fan-out events/s (2017), up to 500k sessions per VM, and a messages cluster of 72 ScyllaDB nodes holding trillions of messages (2022). Replica counts other than ScyllaDB are estimates.

product: Channel message send and real-time delivery
summary: A client posts a message to the Hack webapp, which saves it and hands it to a stateless Admin Server. The Admin Server uses a consistent-hash ring to find the stateful Channel Server that owns the channel. That Channel Server pushes the message to every subscribed Gateway Server worldwide, and each Gateway forwards it over WebSockets to connected clients.

scale.notes: Estimate for message/event sends per second. Sources give tens of millions of connected clients, ~16M channels per Channel Server host at peak, ~500 ms global delivery, and Flannel peaks of 4M connections and 600K client queries/s. Message persistence store and job queue are general knowledge (estimate). Replica counts are estimates.

summary: A merchant's POST passes through Stripe's API tier, where Redis-backed token-bucket limiters and load shedders protect capacity. Requests carry an idempotency key so retries never double-charge. The payments service stores state in DocDB, Stripe's sharded MongoDB-based database: Go proxies route each query to the right shard using a chunk metadata service. The charge is authorised with external card networks, and every database write streams as change events to Kafka for downstream consumers.

scale.notes: Estimate for charge-path API requests at peak, such as Black Friday. Sources: DocDB serves over 5M queries/s across 2,000+ shards with 99.999% uptime, and Stripe processed $1T in payment volume in 2023. Replica counts are estimates.
